title: Ashtavakra's Triumph
body:
Ashtavakra's Triumph

समं पश्यन्हि सर्वत्र समवस्थितमीश्वरम् ।
न हिनस्त्यात्मनात्मानं ततो याति परां गतिम् ।।

"Those, who see God as the Supreme Soul equally present everywhere and in all living beings, do not degrade themselves by their mind. Thereby, they reach the supreme destination. (Gita XIII-28)"

As the Pandavas wandered through the forest of Mithila, Lomasa narrated the story of the young sage Ashtavakra. Ashtavakra was born with eight deformities in his physical body, a result of a curse from his scholarly father Kagola, whom Ashtavakra had corrected from within the womb during a Vedic recitation. Despite his broken physical frame, Ashtavakra's intellect was a peerless mirror of absolute, non-dualistic realization (Jnana).
At the age of twelve, Ashtavakra journeyed to King Janaka's court to defeat the arrogant scholar Vandi, who had drowned many defeated pandits in the ocean, including Ashtavakra's father. When the king's retinue commanded him to make way, Ashtavakra rebuked them: 'Even the king must make way for the deformed, the blind, the fair sex, and those who carry the light of the Vedas.' When Janaka's court pandits laughed at his twisted limbs, Ashtavakra retorted with supreme dignity: 'I thought this was an assembly of scholars, but I see it is a gathering of cobblers (charmakaras) who judge a man by his skin rather than his soul.'
Ashtavakra silenced Vandi in a profound debate on the nature of the One and the Many, proving his absolute mastery over the Vedanta. Vandi admitted defeat, revealing himself as the son of Varuna, and restored all the drowned scholars back to life. Ashtavakra's triumph stands as a beautiful critique of superficial human judgment, proving that the eternal soul is completely unaffected by the limitations and deformities of its material vehicle.
